entry: Biological, chemical, radiological, nuclear or other weapon that can kill or significantly harm many people. Originally coined for aerial bombing with conventional explosives during World War II, the term now usually refers to large-scale biological, chemical, radiological and nuclear weapons, and its scope is disputed and often more political than technical. In World War II the United States developed nuclear weapons and used them twice, in the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. Nazi Germany's use of gases during the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] killed approximately three million people, the largest death toll from chemical weapons in history. During the [[Cold War]], the [[Soviet Union]] and the United States ran the largest nuclear, chemical and biological weapons programs in history. The [[Tokyo subway sarin attack|1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack]] and the [[September 11 attacks]] heightened concern about weapons of mass destruction and terrorism. Claims by a US-led coalition that Iraq was maintaining such programs were a major justification for the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]].

Small predatory [[Mammal|mammal]] of the genus *Mustela* in the family [[Mustelidae]]. Weasels have long, slender bodies and short legs, and are active predators. The genus includes the least weasel, [[Stoat|stoats]], [[Ferret|ferrets]] and European mink, and the wider family includes [[Badger|badgers]], [[Otter|otters]] and wolverines. Least weasels vary in length from 173 to 217 mm and usually have red or brown upper coats and white bellies, though some populations of some species turn wholly white in winter. Weasels feed mainly on small mammals and eat large numbers of [[Rodent|rodents]], but they have been considered vermin because some species took poultry from farms or rabbits from commercial warrens. Their range spans Europe, North America, much of Asia and small areas of North Africa.

Application of science and technology to predict atmospheric conditions for a given location and time. People attempted informal weather prediction for thousands of years, and formal prediction since the 19th century. The Babylonians predicted weather from cloud patterns and [[Astrology|astrology]] as early as 650 BC. Forecasts are made by collecting data on the current state of the atmosphere, land and ocean and applying [[Meteorology|meteorology]] to project changes. Forecasts were once calculated manually from [[Pressure|barometric pressure]], current conditions and cloud cover; today computer models dominate, though people still choose the best model. Accuracy falls as the forecast range grows, because the atmosphere is chaotic and measurements are imperfect, and ensembles and model consensus help narrow the error. Weather warnings protect lives and property, and forecasts of temperature and precipitation are important to agriculture and commodity traders. In 2009 the United States spent approximately $5.8 billion on forecasting, with benefits estimated at six times that amount.

Boundary separating [[Air mass|air masses]] that differ in density, wind, temperature and [[Humidity|humidity]]. Disturbed, unstable weather often develops along it. Cold fronts can bring bands of [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]] and cumulonimbus [[Precipitation|precipitation]] or be preceded by squall lines, while warm fronts are usually preceded by stratiform precipitation and [[Fog|fog]]. Some fronts produce no precipitation and little cloudiness, though there is invariably a wind shift. Cold fronts generally move from west to east and warm fronts poleward, although any direction is possible. Cold fronts move faster than warm fronts because the dense air behind them can lift the warmer air ahead. Occluded fronts combine the two, and stationary fronts stall. Where the density contrast has diminished, for example after air flows over a uniformly warm ocean, a front can degenerate into a shear line, separating regions of differing wind velocity.

Deterioration of [[Soil|soils]], rocks and [[Mineral|minerals]] through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living organisms. Weathering occurs in situ, with little or no movement, and is distinct from [[Erosion|erosion]], which transports material by water, ice, wind, waves and gravity. Physical weathering breaks rock apart mechanically through heat, water, ice and wind, while chemical weathering involves reactions with water, atmospheric gases and biologically produced chemicals; water is the principal agent in both. Frost weathering is the most important form of physical weathering, and a growing body of work suggests that ice segregation, in which water migrates into ice lenses within rock, is more important than the long-favored frost wedging. Atmospheric oxygen, [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and organisms are also important. Weathered material combines with organic matter to form soil, and weathering, erosion and redeposition shape many landforms. [[Sedimentary rock]], a product of weathering, covers 66% of Earth's continents and much of the ocean floor.

Method of [[Textile|textile]] production in which two sets of [[Yarn|yarns]] are interlaced at right angles to form cloth. The longitudinal threads are the warp and the lateral threads the weft, also called woof or filling. The pattern of interlacing, called the weave, determines the cloth's character; most woven products use plain, satin or twill weave. Cloth is usually woven on a [[Loom|loom]], which holds the warp taut while the weft is passed through it. Weaving repeats three primary motions of the loom: shedding, which separates the warp threads to form a clear space called the shed; picking, which propels the weft across; and beating-up, which pushes the weft against the fell of the cloth with a reed. Secondary motions let off the warp and take up the fabric at a regulated rate, and stop motions halt the loom if a thread breaks.

Application for accessing [[Website|websites]] by retrieving and displaying their pages. Browsers fetch text, style sheets, images and other content from a web server over [[HTTP]] or its encrypted form, HTTPS, and a rendering engine converts it into an interactive display. As of 2026 the most used browsers worldwide were [[Google Chrome]], [[Safari (web browser)|Safari]], Edge and [[Firefox]]. The first browser, WorldWideWeb, was created by [[Tim Berners-Lee]]. [[Internet Explorer]], launched by Microsoft in 1995, sparked a browser war with Netscape Navigator and reached a market share of over 95% in the early 2000s. A browser is not the same as a search engine, although the two are often confused.

Colors used in displaying web pages, specified as RGB triplets, hex codes or, in some cases, common English names. Each color is described by the intensity of its red, green and blue components, each stored in eight [[Bit|bits]], giving 24 bits and 16,777,216 colors within the sRGB gamut. In [[Hexadecimal|hexadecimal]] notation this is six digits, usually prefixed by a number sign (#), and some contexts add two digits for transparency. [[CSS|Cascading Style Sheets]] can specify colors outside sRGB with negative or greater-than-100% values, which the hexadecimal syntax cannot express.

Creation and maintenance of websites, spanning [[Graphic design|graphic design]], user interface and user experience design, and search engine optimization. The term usually describes front-end design, including writing [[HTML|markup]], and designers are expected to understand usability and accessibility. A hypertext project that [[Tim Berners-Lee]] proposed at [[CERN]] in 1989 became the [[World Wide Web]]. Early sites were structured with table tags, and the [[Web browser|browser]] Mosaic, created by [[Marc Andreessen]] and Eric Bina in 1993, broke the mold by integrating images and other graphic elements. The W3C was founded in October 1994 to develop common standards, and from 1996 to 1999 browser competition drove rapid development of style sheets, JavaScript and Dynamic HTML.

Set of one or more web pages published under a common domain name and served from a web server. Websites are typically dedicated to a purpose such as news, education, commerce, entertainment or [[Social media|social media]], and are usually known by a common name, often that of the owning organization or brand. They are viewed in a [[Web browser|web browser]], with hyperlinks guiding navigation from a home page. Publicly accessible websites collectively make up the [[World Wide Web]], which is reached over the [[Internet]]; private websites exist only within private networks. The World Wide Web was created in 1989 by [[Tim Berners-Lee]] at [[CERN]]. A static website stores pages on the server in the form sent to the browser, typically coded in [[HTML]] with CSS for appearance, and shows the same content to every visitor. As of July 2026 the most-visited sites were Google, YouTube and Facebook.

Part of the [[Southern Ocean]] bounded by Coats Land and the [[Antarctic Peninsula]]. It contains the Weddell Gyre, and much of its southern part is covered by the Filchner–Ronne [[Ice shelf|ice shelf]]. The sea is around 2,000 kilometers across and covers around 2.8 million square kilometers. Ice shelves on the east side of the Antarctic Peninsula, which once covered roughly 10,000 square kilometers, had disappeared by 2002. Researchers found a Secchi disc visible at 80 meters in October 1986, a clarity matching that of distilled water, and scientists have deemed its water the clearest of any sea. Deep water forms here through cabbeling, a main driver of [[Thermohaline circulation|thermohaline circulation]]. In 1915 the ship *Endurance*, belonging to [[Ernest Shackleton]], was trapped and crushed by ice in the sea; its wreck was found in 2022 at a depth of 3,008 meters.

Ceremony in which two people are united in [[Marriage|marriage]]. Traditions vary greatly between [[Culture|cultures]], religions, countries, social classes and sexual orientations. Most ceremonies include an exchange of vows, a gift such as rings, flowers or money, and a public proclamation of marriage by an authority or celebrant. The white wedding, in which the bride wears a white dress and [[Veil|veil]], was popularized through the marriage of [[Queen Victoria]]. The origin of the wedding ring is unclear, though one possibility is a Roman belief in the vena amoris, a blood vessel said to run from the ring finger to the heart. Receptions often include speeches, the couple's first dance and a wedding cake, and in most of the Western world, as well as [[India]] and [[Malaysia]], guests often throw rice at the newlyweds as they leave.

Triangular [[Tool|tool]], a portable [[Inclined plane|inclined plane]] and one of the six [[Simple machine|simple machines]]. It separates objects, lifts them or holds them in place by converting force applied to its blunt end into forces perpendicular to its inclined surfaces. Its mechanical advantage is the ratio of its slope length to its width, equal to 1/tan α for tip angle α, so a smaller angle gives a greater lifting force. Wedges have existed for thousands of years; the hand axe, made by chipping flint, may be the first example. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] quarries used [[Bronze|bronze]] wedges to split blocks of stone, as well as wooden wedges that swelled when soaked with water. Wedges split wood along the grain, and a narrow gib finely adjusts distances in machine tools. The tips of forks and [[Nail (fastener)|nails]] also act as wedges, and a blade is a compound inclined plane.

A [[Plant|plant]] considered undesirable in a particular situation, growing where it conflicts with human goals. Weeds may be hazardous, unattractive or hard to control in farm fields, orchards, [[Garden|gardens]], lawns and parks, and they can cause major yield losses in agriculture. [[Invasive species]] that harm ecosystems may also be considered weeds. The term has no botanical significance, since a plant is a weed only where it is unwanted, and some plants widely called weeds are deliberately grown as beneficial weeds. Weeds share traits that let them thrive in disturbed environments and resist eradication, and agricultural weeds have co-evolved with [[Crop|crops]] since agriculture began. Control methods include hand [[Hoe (tool)|hoeing]], powered cultivation, mulching, burning, herbicides and crop rotation. Before 1200 AD there is little evidence of concern about weed control, and the [[Bible]] refers to thorns and thistles.

Unit of time equal to seven days, the standard calendrical period between a day and a [[Month|month]] in most parts of the world. There are just over 52 weeks in a year, or on average 4⅓ weeks in a month. Days of the week set work days, rest days and holy days. Ancient cultures used other lengths, including a ten-day week in Egypt and an eight-day week for the Etruscans and ancient Romans. The Romans later adopted a seven-day planetary week, which merged with the Christian week centered on Sunday. In AD 321 [[Constantine the Great|Emperor Constantine]] decreed a seven-day week in the [[Roman Empire]], including Sunday as a public holiday. Today [[Christians]] observe the Sabbath on Sunday, [[Muslims]] on Friday and [[Jews]] on Saturday. Apart from daylight saving time transitions and leap seconds, one week equals 168 hours, 10,080 minutes or 604,800 seconds.

Weekly *shōnen* [[Manga|manga]] anthology magazine published in Japan by Shueisha. It was first released on July 11, 1968, and is one of the longest-running manga magazines. Its circulation peaked at 6.53 million copies a week between the mid-1980s and mid-1990s, when it had a total readership of about 18 million in Japan; in 2021 it averaged over 1.3 million copies a week. The magazine has sold more than 7.5 billion copies since 1968, making it the best-selling comic or manga magazine. Many best-selling series, including *One Piece*, *Dragon Ball*, *Naruto* and *Demon Slayer*, began in its pages. Its sister publications include *Jump SQ*, *V Jump* and the digital *Shōnen Jump+*, and it has spawned a crossover franchise that includes [[Anime|anime]] and video games.

Superfamily of [[Beetle|beetles]] known for the long snout, or rostrum, of its members. Weevils are usually less than 6 mm long and [[Herbivore|herbivorous]], and about 97,000 species are known. Most belong to the family Curculionidae, the true weevils. Many are pests: the grain or wheat weevil damages stored grain, and the boll weevil lays its eggs inside [[Cotton|cotton]] bolls, where its larvae eat their way out. Other weevils are used to control invasive plants biologically. The rostrum carries chewing mouthparts, which excavate tunnels in grain, and most weevils can fly, though some are flightless and others can jump. *Austroplatypus incompertus* is one of the few insects outside the [[Hymenoptera]] and termites (Isoptera) to exhibit eusociality.

American rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1992. Its self-titled debut, known as the *Blue Album*, was released in 1994 and became a multi-platinum success on singles including "Undone – The Sweater Song". The 1996 album *Pinkerton* was a commercial failure but later gained cult status. After a hiatus, the band returned in 2001 with the more pop-oriented *Green Album*, a commercial success. The *Red Album* (2008) produced "Pork and Beans". Weezer has sold more than 35 million albums worldwide, and its 20th album, the *Gold Album*, was released in 2026.

Unified armed forces of Nazi Germany, comprising the *Heer* (army), *Kriegsmarine* (navy) and *Luftwaffe* (air force). It replaced the Reichswehr and was the regime's means of rearming Germany beyond the limits of the [[Treaty of Versailles]]. Its combined-arms tactics achieved rapid victories early in [[World War II]], but overextended fronts could not withstand the Allies' superior numbers and materials. About 18 million men served in it during the war, and German forces lost approximately 11,300,000 men by May 1945. Working closely with the SS, it committed numerous war crimes, and few of its upper leaders were tried for them.

Real-valued function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere. Named after [[Karl Weierstrass]], it was published in 1872 as the first example built specifically to challenge the belief that every continuous function is differentiable except at isolated points. Weierstrass originally defined it as a [[Fourier series]], and it is also an example of a [[Fractal|fractal]] curve. [[Charles Hermite]] called the class of functions with this property a "lamentable scourge". Such functions gained wide acceptance only after computers made them visible and models of [[Brownian motion]] required infinitely jagged curves.

Device for measuring the [[Weight|weight]] or [[Mass|mass]] of an object, also called a balance. The traditional scale has two pans hung at equal distances from a fulcrum, with known weights added to one pan until the pans level. A [[Spring (device)|spring]] scale instead measures how far a spring of known stiffness extends, as described by [[Hooke's law]]. Some scales are calibrated to read in [[Newton (unit)|newtons]], a unit of force, rather than [[Kilogram|kilograms]]. The earliest attested evidence for weighing scales dates to Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, with deben balance weights from the reign of Sneferu (c. 2600 BC). Until the seventeenth century all scales were variations on the balance, and governments were preoccupied with standardizing weights and ensuring traders used them correctly.

Quantity associated with the [[Gravity|gravitational]] [[Force|force]] acting on an object, measured in [[Newton (unit)|newtons]] in the SI system. Textbooks differ on whether weight is a vector or a scalar, or the reaction force that counteracts gravity and is measured by a spring scale; in free fall, by the last definition, weight is zero. An object with a [[Mass|mass]] of one kilogram weighs about 9.8 newtons on Earth and about one-sixth as much on the [[Moon]]. Although weight and mass are distinct, the terms are often confused in everyday use. The concept has been debated for centuries: [[Plato]] saw weight as the natural tendency of objects to seek their kin, and [[Aristotle]] tied it to falling motion. Under the [[Theory of relativity|theory of relativity]], gravity is a consequence of spacetime curvature, and several concepts of weight now coexist.

Reduction of total body mass through loss of fluid, body fat or lean mass. It may be unintentional, resulting from malnourishment or disease, or a deliberate effort to improve overweight or [[Obesity|obese]] status. Unexplained loss not caused by reduced intake or increased exercise, called cachexia, can signal a serious medical condition. Weight loss typically occurs when fewer [[Calorie|calories]] are consumed than are expended. It is the main treatment for obesity, and substantial evidence shows that a 7–10% loss can prevent progression from prediabetes to type 2 [[Diabetes|diabetes]]. It could also reduce pain in people with [[Osteoarthritis|osteoarthritis]] of the knee. Most dieters regain weight over the long term, and a combination of dieting and [[Exercise|exercise]] gives the best results. The [[World Health Organization]] recommends reducing processed foods high in saturated fats, sugar and salt.

German republic from 1918 to 1933, named after the city where its constituent assembly met. It emerged from the German revolution, the abdication of [[Wilhelm II]] and the defeat in [[World War I]]. Hyperinflation and political extremism beset its early years, but monetary and political stability returned by 1924, and the republic joined the [[League of Nations]] in 1926. The [[Great Depression]] brought high unemployment and the collapse of the grand coalition government, followed by presidential cabinets. On 30 January 1933 [[Paul von Hindenburg|Hindenburg]] appointed [[Adolf Hitler]] chancellor. The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act of 1933 gave Hitler broad powers, and a one-party dictatorship followed.

Fabrication process that joins materials, usually [[Metal|metals]] or thermoplastics, by melting the parts so they fuse as they cool. Unlike [[Soldering|soldering]] and brazing, which do not melt the base metal, welding typically adds filler material to form a weld pool. Shielding protects the molten metal from contamination and oxidation. Heat sources include a gas flame, an electric arc, a [[Laser|laser]], an electron beam, friction and [[Ultrasound|ultrasound]]. Welding is hazardous, requiring precautions against burns, electric shock and ultraviolet radiation. Forge welding was the only process until the late 19th century, after which arc and oxy–fuel welding emerged and the world wars accelerated development. Robot welding is now commonplace in industry.
